rationale: A wins because it mostly stays inside the four walls of the update and treats proof gaps like hazards, not confetti. Its line, "the actual price gap between compounded and branded product," is exactly the kind of boring, load-bearing fact a real reporter will demand. B has better snap in places, but "Novo Nordisk and Eli Lilly" and "clearest test case yet" smuggle in facts and scale the update did not give it. That is how a decent angle set gets itself sued by reality.
gaps_in_A: "Hims & Hers pairs at-home blood testing with prescribing, betting personalization sells better than price" invents a strategic bet. The update says lab testing personalizes treatment; it does not say personalization is positioned above price.

"Freshly profitable Hims & Hers bets its next act" and "A newly profitable Hims & Hers doubles down" are close cousins. One is investor strategy, one is regulatory risk, but the set is flirting with duplicate wrapping paper.
"gray-market-adjacent story" is loaded beyond the supplied facts. Compounded and unnamed-source are enough; don't add a vibe felony.

"launch draws pushback from branded drugmakers" may imply this specific launch already drew direct pushback. The update only says branded manufacturers have pushed back generally. Tighten the causal claim.
gaps_in_B: "Novo Nordisk" and "Eli Lilly" are named out of nowhere. The update only says branded manufacturers. True-ish background knowledge is still an invented fact in this exercise.
"Ozempic's Price Locked Them Out" turns generic branded-drug prices into a specific brand story. For weight loss, that brand choice is especially sloppy without the update naming it.
"the clearest test case yet" and "entering the space at scale" inflate the facts. The update says Hims is launching access; it does not prove scale or historical primacy.
"Its First Big Move Carries FDA Risk" is unsupported. Recently profitable plus launching a service does not establish this is the first major strategic move after profitability.
